mechanism: SEC EDGAR publishes a daily index of filings, and each Form 4 is an XML document listing an insider's role, transaction code (P for open-market purchase) and size. A cluster is three or more distinct officers or directors filing P-code buys in the same company inside a short window. A forward log records each cluster the day it appears, with a pre-registered rule and a 100-signal bar, then scores the 21-day return against random same-size stocks and SPY.
claim: Clusters of 3+ insider buys beat random same-size US stocks by about 1.3% per 21 days before costs over 24 months, per the vault's backtest.
verdict_question: Can the EDGAR daily index plus Form 4 XML be parsed keyless into a cluster list, and how many 3+ officer or director P-code clusters appeared in the last 30 days?
probe_title: EDGAR Form 4 cluster scan: how many 3+ insider open-market buy clusters appeared in the last 30 days from the public daily index?
one_line: Insider cluster buys leave a public trail on SEC EDGAR; a forward log with a 100-signal bar would show whether the 1.3% edge survives costs.
idea_why: The edge is small and the vault's own numbers say it vanishes after costs, so only a forward log can settle it.
breakdown: Pull form.idx or the daily index from sec.gov (needs a descriptive User-Agent, no key), filter to Form 4, fetch each XML and keep transaction code P by officers and directors. Group by issuer over a rolling window and flag 3+ distinct filers. Commit the rule, window and 100-signal bar before the first logged signal, then log each cluster with entry price from a free daily bar source. Score at 21 days against SPY and random same-size names with the existing permutation-test approach.

mechanism: Review is layered: automated agent reviewers read each change first, human time is rationed to the changes that need it, and the target is the minimum human review that does not raise reverts or incidents. Reverts and incidents are the feedback signal, and fast, easy rollback is part of the design. The reviewer is improved over time from missed bugs.
claim: From June to September merged PRs more than doubled while the share reverted fell by over 40 percent.
why_not_testable: It is an internal process on private repositories, with no public data or tool to run.
needs: Access to a high-volume agent-written repository with revert history.
one_line: Anthropic's Claude Code team moved most code reading to machines and judges review by revert rate; their claim is unverifiable from outside.
idea_why: Using revert rate as the review-quality metric is sensible, but the numbers come from one team's own repository.
breakdown: On a Proteus repo, add an automated reviewer pass on every nightly commit and log reverts and later fixes against it. Compare revert rates with and without the pass over several weeks. A human would still decide which changes always get eyes, such as the hook and charter files.

missing: A repo with enough change volume to make revert rates measurable.

mechanism: Every losing or odd trade in a paper window gets a one-line cause logged within a day, classed as rule change or variance. A cause is only allowed to alter a rule if it recurs, with the change committed before the next window. This stops rules being tuned to single outcomes and shows how much of the loss is noise.
claim: The reel pitches a journal habit; the vault notes only 7 trades and +256 dollars, so no edge evidence.
why_not_testable: It needs a paper window with real losing trades to classify, which does not exist tonight.
needs: A running S1 paper window with at least 20 closed trades.
one_line: A one-line cause per losing trade, labelled rule change or variance, would show how much of a paper window's loss is just noise.
idea_why: Separating variance from rule faults before editing rules is a standard guard against overfitting to single trades.
breakdown: Add a causes column to the paper trade log and write the one-line cause at close. Set a pre-registered threshold, for example the same cause three times, before a rule may change. At window end count rule-change versus variance causes and report the split. No script covers the judgement of what a cause was, so a person or sub-agent writes it.

mechanism: A separate steering agent watches a running agent's context. A cheap fast path decides whether to intervene; a costly slow path writes the intervention. Both paths are trained together with a pairwise ranking objective and GRPO, and the intervention rate can be tuned without retraining.
claim: Improves performance and efficiency of single and multi-agent search systems and transfers to unseen executors.
why_not_testable: It needs RL training and a trained steering model, and there is no local model on this Mac.

one_line: A cheap watcher decides when a long agent run has drifted off its goal, and a costly one writes the correction.
idea_why: A two-tier monitor, cheap to check and costly to intervene, fits how drift actually shows up in long runs.

mechanism: A rule-based retest entry on Nasdaq futures is backtested over a longer span, then compared with random-entry runs of the same trade count to give a luck percentile. The vault's 10-week 15-minute run made +1878 on one MNQ contract at 2R and beat 95 percent of random runs. Two years of 1-hour bars give far more trades before any claim.
claim: A 10-week NQ 15m backtest gave +1878 on 1 MNQ at 2R and beat 95 percent of random runs.
verdict_question: On two years of keyless 1h NQ=F bars, does the retest rule beat 95 percent of random-entry runs with the same trade count?
probe_title: Retest rule on 2 years of NQ 1h bars: does it still beat 95% of random-entry runs?
one_line: The 10-week Nasdaq retest rule beat 95 percent of random runs; two years of hourly bars will say whether that was luck.
idea_why: Ten weeks is too short to separate an edge from luck, and a longer sample is the cheap, decisive check.
breakdown: Pull about 730 days of 1h NQ=F bars via yfinance, which allows that span keyless. Encode the 8 Oct retest rule exactly as written in the vault, run it with 2R targets, then run a few thousand random-entry simulations with matching trade count and the same exits. Use the backtest-with-luck-test skill for the permutation step. Report net result, trade count and luck percentile, with the rule frozen before the run.
